title: Projected Confidence Does Not Always Come From the Inside
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece distinguishes between the inner confidence a leader possesses and the confidence a leader projects to others. It argues that inner confidence is not innate but built through experience, with success in one arena carrying over into related ones and creating momentum. The article then makes its key move: possessing confidence does not guarantee projecting it, and projection is a separate skill that matters equally for success. Displaying the social markers of confidence both boosts inner confidence and makes the leader more believable, because people infer expertise from the cues experts naturally use. The piece closes with a short list of such markers, including emotional language, vivid words, strong qualifiers, direct eye contact, diverse word choice and purposeful gestures, and urges leaders to use them deliberately when persuading.
points: Inner confidence is described as a muscle built through attempting new things and overcoming obstacles, not an innate trait.
Confidence gained in one domain, such as public speaking, carries over into related activities like small-group facilitation, creating compounding momentum.
Projecting confidence is treated as a distinct skill: displaying its markers both strengthens inner confidence and makes the leader more credible to others.

Because audiences infer expertise from the cues genuine experts use, leaders can deliberately employ emotional language, vivid descriptors, strong qualifiers, eye contact and purposeful gestures to be believed.
quotes: The inner confidence leaders possess is not innate but born of experience. The more we attempt new things and learn how to overcome the obstacles inherent in them, the more we build the confidence muscle.

High confidence in one arena, say speaking, leads to higher confidence in related endeavors, such as small group conversations or facilitation. Inner confidence grows when we experience and learn in more areas.
Projecting confidence is a whole other animal and equally important to success. Interestingly, when we display the markers or cues of high confidence, two things happen.
When leaders exhibit the markers of confidence, others come to believe they know and are worth believing. This works because people infer from what they do that they are the expert.

So, any time we use those same social markers, others feel our confidence and presume we really know. Learning to use the markers of confidence intentionally is something all good leaders should invest in.
When we are truly the expert, we use these cues profusely. Using them any time we want to persuade others helps us to be believed.
